paragraphs: Vyasa was one of India's greatest sages, the author of the Vedanta aphorisms and a deeply holy man. His father, grandfather and great-grandfather had each tried to reach spiritual perfection and fallen short. Vyasa himself did not fully succeed either, but his son Shuka was born perfect.

Vyasa taught Shuka the knowledge of truth, and then sent him to the court of King Janaka for further teaching. Janaka was called Videha, "without a body", because, king though he was, he had completely forgotten he was a body and lived always as the spirit.

Janaka knew Vyasa's son was coming and prepared a test. When Shuka arrived at the palace gates, the guards ignored him. They offered him a seat and nothing more. For three days and nights he sat there, and no one spoke to him or asked who he was. The son of a sage revered across the land was treated as a nobody by the gatekeepers.

Then everything changed. The king's ministers and high officials suddenly appeared, welcomed him with great honour and led him into magnificent rooms. For eight days he enjoyed fragrant baths, fine clothes and every luxury. Through all of it, Shuka's calm face never shifted, not even slightly. He was the same in the palace as he had been at the gate.

Finally he was brought before the king, who sat on his throne amid music, dancing and entertainment. Janaka handed him a cup filled to the very brim with milk and asked him to walk seven times around the hall without spilling a drop. Shuka took the cup and moved through the music and the lovely faces. Seven times he circled, and not one drop fell. Nothing in the world could pull at his mind unless he allowed it.

When he returned the cup, the king told him there was nothing more to teach. All Janaka could do was repeat what Shuka's father had taught and what Shuka had already realised. "You have known the Truth; go home."
learn: Insult and flattery both try to pull you off balance; real maturity is staying steady through either. Shuka's cup of milk is a great picture of focus: the world can be loud and dazzling, and you can still keep your mind on what you're carrying.
